summary: Morgante Pell founded Grit to address a gap he observed at Google Cloud: 90% of customers needed help running existing applications, not building new ones. Most AI demos show greenfield app creation, but developers spend their time modifying huge applications. Pell identifies three categories of developer tools: IDE assistance (most product-market fit, simple autocomplete), AI agents lowering the floor for non-technical users (skeptical), and Grit's focus on raising the ceiling for top engineers. Principal engineers are limited by time; AI agents can be in ten places at once. At Grit's customers, 95% of engineers never touch Grit—one engineer drives hundreds of PRs with agents. The core process has three steps: planning (semantic embeddings plus traditional static analysis indexing), execution (LLMs delegate to sub-agents using a custom query engine called gql and diff generation), and PR review. gql combines syntactic queries, semantic similarity via embeddings, and dependency graph traversal. A naive RAG approach fails because it retrieves irrelevant context and can't handle unpredictable result sizes. Even Claude 3.5 Sonnet produces code that looks correct but is wrong—demonstrating why compilers and type checking remain essential verification systems. Compilers like TSC ground LLMs by catching type errors that neither humans nor models can detect by inspection. However, enterprise codebases take 10+ minutes to build, dwarfing inference time. Grit solves this by using language servers (like TS server) for incremental rechecking in seconds rather than full builds. Agents also fail due to compounding errors in loops—more than 10 consecutive prompts dramatically lower success rates. Grit addresses this with checkpoint-revert strategies and Firecracker VM snapshots to fork in-memory state into 6-10 parallel agent environments, creating a distributed-database-like architecture where agents vote on quorum state. For edit formatting, whole-file regeneration is expensive due to output token costs (3-15x input tokens), diffs have line-number accuracy issues, and JSON-escaped function calls waste tokens. Grit's gql loose search-and-replace format uses before/after snippets with fuzzy matching, avoiding these pitfalls. Pell envisions a future Sim City-like UI for managing entire codebases at multiple zoom levels.

sections.title: Motivation and Background
sections.summary: Pell introduces himself as founder of Grit, explaining his Google Cloud background and the insight that customers need tools for existing applications, not new ones. He frames Grit's mission as raising the ceiling for top engineers.

sections.title: Tool Categories and Product Strategy
sections.summary: Pell categorizes developer tools into IDE assistance, AI agents lowering the floor, and tools raising the ceiling. Grit targets the latter, supercharging principal engineers who are limited by time. 95% of engineers at customers don't touch Grit.

sections.title: The Need for Bulldozers for Code
sections.summary: Current IDEs are scalpels for individual lines. With 20-30% more code being generated, tools need to handle bulk changes across hundreds of repos—bulldozers for code.

sections.title: OpenTelemetry Migration Case Study
sections.summary: A customer with thousands of repos migrated from logging to OpenTelemetry. Traditionally a massive coordination effort, Grit completed it in under 100 developer hours in one week after it had been postponed for years.

sections.title: Three-Step Process: Planning, Execution, Review
sections.summary: Grit indexes code semantically and via static analysis, then executes plans by delegating to sub-agents using gql and diff generation, then pushes PRs for review by principal engineers.

sections.title: gql Query Engine and RAG Limitations
sections.summary: Naive RAG fails for finding code to modify due to irrelevant context and unpredictable thresholds. gql combines syntactic queries, semantic similarity via embeddings, and dependency graph traversal for precise code identification.

sections.title: LLM Reliability Limitations and Compiler Grounding
sections.summary: Even Claude 3.5 Sonnet with full context produces code that looks correct but is broken. Compilers like TSC catch these errors and ground the LLM for correction. AI agents need the same compiler and language server tools that make human developers superhuman.

sections.title: Build Times and Language Server Optimization
sections.summary: Enterprise codebases take 10+ minutes to build, dwarfing 30-second inference times. Language servers like TS server enable incremental rechecking in seconds via in-memory indexes, making agentic loops feasible.

sections.title: Compounding Errors and Checkpoint-Revert Strategy
sections.summary: More than 10 consecutive prompts dramatically lower PR success rates due to compounding failures. Grit saves known-good checkpoints, reverts to them when stuck, and uses Firecracker VM snapshots to fork in-memory state into 6-10 parallel environments for quorum voting.

sections.title: Edit Format Economics and gql Loose Search-and-Replace
sections.summary: Whole-file regeneration is expensive (output tokens 3-15x input cost), diffs have line-number accuracy issues, and JSON-escaped function calls waste tokens. Grit's gql loose search-and-replace uses before/after snippets with fuzzy matching, inspired by tutorial-style replacements.

sections.title: Future Vision and Closing
sections.summary: Pell envisions a Sim City-like UI for managing entire codebases at multiple zoom levels. Grit is hiring.
